Historically the ''kuri'' was a kitchen which prepared meals only for the abbot and his guests, though in modern {{ill|Japan|en|Japan|qid=Q17|lt=Japan}} it now functions as the kitchen and administrative office for the entire monastery.<ref name="baroni">Baroni, 201</ref><ref>Watanabe, 34</ref>

{{translated page|ja|庫裏|version=82636972|comment=Imported full ja history}}

'''Kuri''' (くり) is one of the {{jalink|伽藍|Q3482038|garan}} (temple buildings) in {{jalink|仏教|Q748|Buddhist}} {{jalink|寺院|Q5393308|temples}}. It is also written as '''庫裡'''. 裡 is a colloquial character for 裏, and both mean “inside” or “within”. It is also called '''kuin'''.

== Overview ==
It is the place where {{jalink|僧侶|monks}} of the temple reside, and also serves as a place to prepare meals within the temple, functioning as a kitchen. In modern times, it more often refers to the place where monks reside.

In large-scale temples, the ''kuri'' is an independent building, but in ordinary temples it often doubles as the temple office that handles temple affairs. Many buildings closely resemble ordinary private homes.

In temples with historical significance, some are designated as {{jalink|文化財|Q858308|cultural properties}}. In {{jalink|禅宗|Q7953|Zen}} temples, {{jalink|韋駄天|Q2006388|Idaten}} is sometimes enshrined as the guardian of the garan.

== Large Kuri and Small Kuri ==
In {{jalink|禅寺|Zen temples}}, centered around scholar monks, it is a place where meals for resident monks and offerings to the Buddha are prepared, and it also serves as the monks' hall. This is called ''daikuri'' (large kuri) or ''daikuin'' (large hall). In contrast, that which is established near the ''{{jalink|方丈|Q96028062|hōjō}}'' building is called ''shōkuri'' (small kuri) or ''shōkuin'' (small hall), and refers to the kitchen for the abbot's attendants and guest quarters.
